summary:
Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity under its penal code, and the provision has been used against people whose conduct became known to authorities. Reported penalties differ between sources: Outright International gives Article 300 of the 2020 penal code as six months to two years' imprisonment plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs (US$240 to 720), the Human Dignity Trust states a maximum of three years, and a December 2024 Washington Blade report cites Article 318 carrying up to five years.

Enforcement is documented. Two women were arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them, and on 12 December 2024 a Comorian court sentenced them to five and six months respectively for homosexuality before releasing them with the terms served. It was the first conviction of this kind, and the Human Dignity Trust called it a human-rights violation. The first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy followed a leaked video in 2022.

Application is uneven rather than absent. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report records no arrests or prosecutions during that year and states that authorities did not actively enforce the law. The statute itself remains in force, and the government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise.

No non-discrimination law protects LGBTQI+ persons. Police reported that they do not incite or tolerate violence against them and no such violence was reported in 2023, yet widespread impunity is listed among the country's major human-rights problems.

Detention carries additional exposure: the State Department's 2010 report records poor prison conditions, alongside restrictions on movement, press and religion and discrimination against women.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so a trans visitor arriving with documents in a retained name or marker has no domestic route to a matching record. No hate-crime provision or partner recognition for same-sex couples is recorded in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
Source reporting on the penalty does not converge, which matters when a visitor weighs the consequence of a charge. The Human Dignity Trust profile states up to three years, Outright International specifies six months to two years plus a fine under Article 300 of the 2020 code, and the Washington Blade report on the December 2024 sentencing cites Article 318 with a five-year maximum.

The enforcement picture shifts across reporting years. The 2010 State Department report offers little on LGBT issues while documenting poor prison conditions and general restrictions; the 2023 report describes non-enforcement; the 2022 leaked-video imprisonment, the June 2024 arrests and the December 2024 conviction show that prosecutions do occur when cases surface.

Police posture reported in 2023, namely no incitement or toleration of violence and no reported incidents, sits alongside the State Department's finding of widespread impunity, so the absence of recorded violence does not establish a protective framework.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal mechanism to change the gender marker on official documents, and no non-discrimination statute covers LGBTQI+ persons.

No LGBTIQ organisations are known to operate in Comoros. Article 5 of Law 86-006/AF deters registration, so organising has no lawful channel.

The government has repeatedly declined United Nations recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct, indicating that the legal position is a settled policy choice rather than an unenforced leftover.
outOfScopeNotes:
The applicable penalty is unresolved in these sources: three years, two years plus a fine, and five years are each reported, and the discrepancy is not reconciled by any source in the inventory.

The enforcement position after the December 2024 conviction is not sourced. The inventory contains no reporting on arrests, prosecutions or police practice in 2025 or 2026, so the current enforcement posture beyond that date is not established here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of transgender documents, airport or border treatment, access to healthcare, restroom or facility rules, hate-crime charging, or recognition of same-sex partners. These are not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

The 2010 prison-conditions findings are more than a decade old and have not been refreshed in the inventory.
